stem: An ICSR differs from a clinical case report in that:
options: It is structured around standardized data elements with regulated submission timelines
It contains only confirmed adverse drug reactions
It cannot be modified once created
rationale: The ICSR is a regulatory artifact with structured data elements (E2B), bound submission timelines, and full audit trail. A is incorrect — ICSRs can be lengthy. C is incorrect — ICSRs include suspected reactions and adverse events. D is incorrect — ICSRs are routinely updated through follow-up cycles.

stem: Which document defines the data elements and electronic message specification used to transmit an ICSR between sender and regulator?
rationale: E2B(R3) is the implementation guide for ICSR data elements and message structure. E2A defines clinical safety standards; E2D covers postmarket reporting principles; E2F is the DSUR.

stem: A sales representative learns of a serious adverse event from a physician at a conference. The reporting clock for this case starts:
options: When the case is entered into the safety database
When the sales representative returns to the office
On the date of the conference conversation
When the QPPV signs off on the validity assessment
rationale: Day Zero is the date the company first becomes aware of a valid case through any employee or contracted party. Internal routing delays do not pause or reset the clock.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a downstream function of the ICSR?
rationale: ICSR data does not feed pricing decisions. The other three are core PV functions.

stem: The minimum data needed for a valid ICSR includes:
options: A confirmed diagnosis, named reporter, suspect drug, and lab confirmation
An identifiable patient, identifiable reporter, suspect product, and suspect event
A serious adverse event, signed informed consent, dechallenge result, and reporter qualification
A complete medical history, current medication list, suspect drug, and event onset date
rationale: The four validity elements are minimal — identifiable patient, identifiable reporter, suspect product, and suspect event. Confirmed diagnoses, lab values, and complete histories are desirable but not required for validity.

stem: A patient enrolled in a company-sponsored disease management program reports a headache to the program nurse during a routine check-in call. This is classified as:
rationale: The disease management program is an organized data collection activity. Reports arising from such programs are solicited per GVP VI.

stem: Under GVP VI, the minimum required cadence for systematic literature surveillance in major databases is:
rationale: Weekly is the minimum cadence specified in GVP VI for active substance literature surveillance.

stem: A sponsor receives an extract of cases from FAERS containing twelve cases involving its product. Five of these are duplicates of cases already in the sponsor's database. The correct action is:
options: Submit all twelve cases as new ICSRs
Reject the FAERS extract because duplicates indicate an FDA error
Reconcile against the existing database, link duplicates, and process only the genuinely new cases
Wait for FDA to clarify the duplicates
rationale: Reconciliation against existing cases is mandatory; the E2B framework supports this through worldwide unique case identifiers.

stem: Causality on a solicited case is:
options: Assessed by the HCP, like a clinical trial case
Decided by the company medical reviewer with no reporter input
rationale: Solicited cases are treated like clinical study reports — causality is HCP-assessed, not assumed.

stem: A company's branded Twitter account is actively monitored. A patient posts about a serious adverse event. Day Zero is:
options: The date of the patient's Twitter post
The date the medical information team identifies the post
The date the patient followed up with their doctor
The end of the calendar week
rationale: Day Zero for digital media monitoring is the date of company identification of the relevant content.

stem: Which of the following constitutes the minimum for an identifiable patient under ICH validity criteria?
options: Full name and date of birth
Patient identification number assigned by the reporting institution
Demographic descriptors sufficient to distinguish this patient from others (e.g., age, sex)
A signed authorization from the patient
rationale: Patient identifiability requires distinguishing demographic information; full name and DOB are not required.

stem: A consumer reports an AE but refuses to provide contact information. Three follow-up attempts via the original communication channel are unsuccessful. The correct action is:
options: Treat the case as valid using the originally submitted information
Hold as pending invalid; close after a defined period if validity is never achieved
Submit the case to FAERS as anonymous
rationale: Pending invalid status with documented follow-up attempts; closure occurs only after the defined SOP period (commonly 90 days).

stem: A serious case is identified independently in the company database from three sources: patient call, regulator extract, and HCP report. Day Zero is:
options: The earliest of the three source dates
The latest of the three source dates
The date the third source confirms the case
The date the medical reviewer determines all three describe the same case
rationale: Day Zero attaches to the earliest company awareness of the valid case, regardless of how many additional sources later confirm it.

stem: Validity criteria are required for an ICSR because:
options: They define the threshold at which the reporting clock starts and the case enters regulatory submission obligations
They are required by US 21 CFR but not by EU GVP
They distinguish serious from non-serious cases
rationale: Validity is the regulatory gate for clock initiation and submission obligation, harmonized across ICH regions.

stem: Which of the following would render a case invalid?
options: Suspect product administered three years before the report
rationale: The event must be describable in terms allowing MedDRA coding. ZIP code is not required; reporter qualification is not strictly required (especially for consumer reports); time elapsed since exposure does not invalidate.

stem: Day Zero on a postmarket spontaneous case is:
options: The date the safety database creates the case record
The earliest date any company employee or contractually bound party became aware of the valid case
The date the QPPV signs off
The date of the adverse event
rationale: Day Zero anchors to the earliest awareness of a valid case anywhere in the company organization.

stem: A French affiliate receives a serious AE report on Friday and forwards it to the global safety database the following Tuesday. The reporting clock for global submission:
options: Started when the global database received the case
Started Friday and is now four days into the clock
Resets when the case is QC'd
rationale: Internal routing delays do not pause the clock; the clock started at the affiliate's awareness on Friday.

stem: A 15-day case under US 21 CFR 314.80 must be submitted within:
options: 15 calendar days of Day Zero, with weekends and holidays counted
15 working days of receipt by the safety database
rationale: Calendar days are the standard; weekends and holidays count.

stem: Which of the following triggers a new expedited reporting clock?
options: A typographical correction to the narrative
Death added as outcome on a previously non-fatal serious case
A new lab value reported within reference range
rationale: Significant follow-up information — particularly outcome upgrades to fatal — triggers a new expedited submission with its own clock.

stem: A SUSAR with fatal outcome arising in a US IND study must be submitted in:
rationale: 21 CFR 312.32 requires fatal/life-threatening SUSARs to be submitted within 7 calendar days, with a 15-day follow-up.

stem: A reporter describes "shortness of breath, chest pain, and a CT-confirmed diagnosis of pulmonary embolism." The correct primary coding is:
options: Dyspnoea + Chest pain + Pulmonary embolism (three PTs)
rationale: Diagnosis preferred over symptoms; code only Pulmonary embolism.

stem: A patient's ALT is reported as 350 U/L (upper limit of normal 56) with no clinical symptoms or diagnosis from the reporter. The correct coding is:
rationale: Without clinical interpretation by the reporter, the lab abnormality is coded as the Investigation PT.

stem: Which of the following is the MedDRA coding level for AE reporting?
rationale: PTs are the reporting level. LLTs are the coding level (reflecting reporter language); the LLT maps to a PT for reporting.

stem: When the reporter states "the patient died" with no cause of death identified, the correct event coding is:
rationale: Death PT is used when no cause is identified. When a cause is known, the cause is coded and the fatal outcome is captured separately.

stem: SMQs (Standardised MedDRA Queries) are primarily used for:
options: Selecting the SOC for an LLT
rationale: SMQs are validated groupings used in signal detection and aggregate analyses, not in individual case coding.

stem: A patient is admitted overnight for an elective knee replacement scheduled six weeks earlier. During the stay, a possible drug-related rash develops but does not extend the stay. The admission itself:
options: Counts toward seriousness because the patient was hospitalized
Does not count, because it was pre-planned for a reason unrelated to the event
Counts toward seriousness because the rash occurred in hospital
Counts toward seriousness only if the rash was severe
rationale: B. A pre-planned admission for a reason unrelated to the event is excluded from the hospitalization criterion. Had the rash prolonged the stay, the prolongation would count. Severity (D) is not a seriousness criterion.

stem: Which of the following events is on the EMA IME list and should generally be considered serious even without hospitalization?
rationale: Bronchospasm with ED intervention is an IME-list event.

stem: Seriousness is assessed at:
options: Event level, with case-level derived from the maximum of event-level
rationale: Event-level assessment, with case-level being the maximum.

stem: A non-serious case is upgraded to serious on follow-up. The new expedited reporting clock starts:
options: From the date of the new information
There is no new clock — the original report stands
rationale: The upgrade triggers a new clock anchored to the date of new information.

stem: "Life-threatening" as a seriousness criterion means:
options: The event could have been fatal if untreated
The patient was at risk of death at the time the event occurred
The event involved cardiovascular or respiratory systems
Any event with potential long-term consequences
rationale: Life-threatening is assessed at the time of the event, not hypothetically.

stem: Severity and seriousness are:
options: Independent dimensions captured separately in the ICSR
Severity is regulatory; seriousness is clinical
rationale: Severity is intensity (clinical); seriousness is regulatory classification.

stem: A reporter rates an event as "severe." The case has no hospitalization, is not life-threatening, and is not on the IME list. The case is:
options: Always serious because severity is severe
Non-serious; severity does not by itself trigger seriousness
Serious only if duration exceeds 7 days
Serious only if reported by an HCP
rationale: Severity does not by itself confer seriousness.

stem: A patient develops a mild rash that subsequently progresses to Stevens-Johnson syndrome. At initial presentation:
options: Severity is mild and seriousness is non-serious
Severity is mild but seriousness is serious due to IME/DME considerations
Severity is severe by definition because SJS is dangerous
rationale: SJS is a DME and IME-list event; the case is serious from initial recognition that SJS is a possibility.

stem: CTCAE Grade 3 events are:
options: Always serious by ICH E2A criteria
Sometimes serious, depending on whether E2A criteria are met
Used only in IND safety reports
rationale: Grade 3 (severe) does not automatically equal serious. Grade 4 (life-threatening) typically does.

stem: Seriousness is determined by:
options: The sponsor / MAH against ICH E2A criteria
rationale: Seriousness is a sponsor / MAH determination, not delegated to the reporter or patient.

stem: A SUSAR is defined as:
options: A serious, unexpected, suspected adverse reaction
A spontaneous, unexpected, severe adverse reaction
rationale: SUSAR = Serious + Unexpected + Suspected to be related.

stem: Per ICH E2D, on a spontaneous report, causality is:
options: Always assessed by the sponsor and never assumed
Implicitly suspected unless explicitly denied by the reporter
Determined only after follow-up with the reporter
rationale: Spontaneous report = implicit suspected relationship unless denied.

stem: A reporter says "probably not related." The sponsor's safety physician concludes "possibly related" based on temporal proximity and lack of alternative cause. The case is reported with causality:
options: As stated by the sponsor (the more conservative position)
rationale: The more conservative (more related) assessment governs reportability; both are captured.

stem: Positive rechallenge means:
options: The drug was readministered and the event recurred
The drug was stopped and the event resolved
The drug was substituted with placebo
rationale: Rechallenge = re-administration; positive rechallenge = recurrence on re-administration.

stem: Confounding by indication refers to:
options: The disease being treated also causing the event
Multiple drugs causing the same event
rationale: Confounding by indication = the disease itself is associated with the outcome, independently of treatment.

stem: A case narrative is written in:
rationale: Past tense, third person, plain medical English.

stem: Lab values in a narrative should be reported with:
options: Numerical value, units, and reference range
rationale: Lab values without units and reference ranges are uninterpretable to the reader.

stem: Which of the following is appropriate language in a case narrative?
options: "There is no evidence of safety concerns"
rationale: Narratives use neutral, factual clinical description.

stem: When a diagnosis is provided by the reporter, the narrative should:
options: Use the diagnosis as the headline event and contextualize symptoms within the diagnosis
Repeat both diagnosis and all symptoms in equal detail
rationale: The diagnosis is the headline; symptoms are contextual.

stem: A pregnancy narrative must include:
options: Exposure timing relative to LMP or gestational age
rationale: Gestational timing of exposure is essential to teratogenicity assessment.

stem: A SUSAR is reportable in:
options: Both settings under the same name
Postmarket only after market authorization withdrawal
rationale: SUSAR is a clinical development term; postmarket uses different terminology (serious + unexpected suspected adverse reaction, but the SUSAR acronym is reserved for trials).

stem: The reference document for expectedness assessment in a clinical trial is:
options: The Reference Safety Information section of the IB
rationale: The RSI is a specific designated section, not the full IB.

stem: Default causality on a postmarket spontaneous report is:
options: Not related, unless reporter says otherwise
Implicitly suspected related, unless reporter explicitly denies
rationale: ICH E2D establishes implicit suspected relationship.

stem: A 7-day reporting clock applies to:
options: All serious cases in the EU
Fatal/life-threatening SUSARs in IND and EU CTR settings
rationale: The 7-day clock is for fatal/life-threatening SUSARs in trial settings.

stem: Aggregate reporting for clinical development uses:
rationale: DSUR is the development-phase aggregate report.

stem: The Pharmacovigilance System Master File (PSMF) is:
options: A document required only at MAH renewal
A continuously updated description of the EU MAH's PV system per GVP Module II
The submission of all PSURs in one volume
The training record of all PV staff
rationale: The PSMF is a continuously maintained "live" document.

stem: Late case investigation requires:
options: Documented root cause analysis with CAPA where indicated
Resubmission of all cases for the calendar year
rationale: Root cause and CAPA are the standard response.

stem: The audit trail must capture:
options: Every change with user, timestamp, and before/after values
rationale: Comprehensive change capture is the standard.

stem: A regulator inspection identifies a critical finding. The most likely consequence is:
options: A note in the inspection report only
Warning letter, consent decree, or marketing suspension
Public disclosure of the company's submission rate
rationale: Critical findings produce significant regulatory action.

stem: Reconciliation between the safety database and an external source (vendor, partner, regulator extract) is intended to:
options: Verify that all valid cases captured externally are present in the safety database
rationale: Reconciliation is the verification mechanism for completeness.
